effect: Hobbes’s authorization is linked to securing peace; I can now test its limit when protection fails.
reaction: The qualification that concentrated power may fail is useful.
reason: Apply the protection failure to Hobbes’s account to address the first goal.
expectation: I expect the loss of protection to qualify the subject’s obligation to obey, though the precise limit may be narrower.

reaction: The distinction makes the limit clearer.
reason: This is the only offered combination and it advances the remaining Locke goal.

effect: Locke’s consent authorizes majority decisions but leaves rulers entrusted with protecting lives, liberty and possessions.
reaction: The distinction between consent and permission for arbitrary seizure is clear.
reason: The only offered combination tests how arbitrary seizure breaches that trust.
expectation: I expect Locke’s account to treat arbitrary seizure as a breach that may justify resistance or ending the rulers’ authority.

effect: Locke’s breach-of-trust account can justify resistance, contrasting with Hobbes’s protection-based limit; neither guarantees success.
reaction: The concrete seizure example makes the contrast useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Testing arbitrary seizure against Locke’s trust was most worthwhile: it made the limits of consent concrete.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial authorization step felt mostly preparatory; its link to peace was brief and predictable.

surprise.text: Hobbes’s duty of obedience can end when protection is lost, not merely when a subject dislikes a decision.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the offered combinations made the route largely prescribed.

continue.text: I would continue: comparing the two limits on authority was clear and gave me a useful distinction to carry forward.
